paras: The lynching of Alex Wilson and Perry Munson took place at Monroe, Louisiana, on the night of August 22-23, 1881, when a mob took the two Black prisoners from the parish jail and hanged them outside town. Both men were held on charges of murdering other Black men and had not been tried. The Monroe papers condemned the killing, and a New Orleans Democrat dispatch carried brief notices of it nationally.

On the night of August 17, Anderson Mitchell, a Black man, was killed by a blow to the neck while walking with his wife at the Kansas plantation on Bayou DeSiard. According to a Monroe dispatch to the Democrat, Perry Munson and a second man were arrested on suspicion. Alex Wilson had been charged about a month earlier with the murder of Reuben Leonard, also Black; the Democrat's correspondent said Wilson had called Leonard out of church and shot him.

Wilson had had a preliminary examination and was committed without bail, while Munson's examination was set for the day after the lynching. The Ouachita Telegraph wrote that the evidence against both men was circumstantial, though "quite strong and convincing," that neither had been proved guilty, and that both were being held for the grand jury.

According to the Monroe Bulletin, a mob broke into the sheriff's office between 11 and 12 o'clock on Monday night, August 22, and took the jail keys. The Democrat's Monroe dispatch put it between 1 and 2 o'clock the next morning. The men took Wilson and Munson from their cells and hanged them near the road to Bayou DeSiard, a mile and a half from town by the dispatch's account and about two and a half miles from the courthouse by the Telegraph's.

Dr. Cage was the only person reported to have seen the mob, and the Bulletin said he had "no idea of its complexion." Some of the men, the Bulletin added, knew just where to find the keys and what tools would force the locks.

The Telegraph called it "horrifying and revolting" that the parish would arrest people and then fail to protect them, and it urged the proper officers to investigate "to the bottom" and make an example of everyone responsible. No report of an inquest, arrests, grand jury action or trial appears in the coverage, and no member of the mob was named.

Outside Louisiana the story came from the Democrat's Monroe special of August 23, which the Sacramento Daily Record-Union printed the next day under "More Negroes Lynched" and the Washington Evening Star as "Two Men Hanged by a Mob." The wire copy named the victims "Perry Mason and Alex Wilson" or "Perry Mason and Alexander Mason," and the Savannah Morning News, headed "Murderers Lynched," printed "Percy Mason." Brief versions also ran in the Independent Statesman on August 25 and the Watertown Republican on August 31.

In north Louisiana the Monroe Bulletin's account, reprinted as "More Mob Law" in the Morehouse Clarion and the Richland Beacon, called such proceedings "indefensible" and harmful to the country. The Ouachita Telegraph headed its report "Hanging by Judge Lynch" and called the act "shameful and disgraceful" and "barbarously cruel," while describing the murders charged to the prisoners as "cold blooded and premeditated." The Bulletin text appeared again in the Louisiana Capitolian on August 30, and on September 1 the Bossier Banner summarized it as the hanging of "two negroes, both charged with murdering men of their own color."

The hour varies: 11 to 12 on Monday night (Bulletin), 1 to 2 on Tuesday morning (Democrat dispatch), about 2 o'clock Tuesday (Independent Statesman), or the night of the 23rd (Bossier Banner). Munson appears as "Perry Munson" in the Monroe papers, "Jerry Munson" in the dispatch printed at Baton Rouge and "Perry Mason" in the national wire; the local papers, written in Monroe after the event, are the closer source. A Telegraph item quoted by the Donaldsonville Chief named the August 17 victim "Anderson Bates" and the second suspect Aaron Anderson, where the earlier dispatch named Anderson Mitchell and "Aaron Buder."

reader.title: Lynching of Alex Wilson and Perry Munson
bases: A mob took two Black prisoners charged with murder from the Monroe jail at night and hanged them outside town (A9, A12, A14).

Both prisoners were hanged by 'a mob' or 'a party of men' with no lawful authority, the Telegraph stressing they had not been proved guilty (A12, A14); the killing answered murder charges against them (A9, A14).
The New Orleans Democrat's Monroe dispatch (A2, A9), the Monroe Bulletin (A13, A14) and the Ouachita Telegraph (A12) independently agree that two Black prisoners were taken from the jail and hanged.
